Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injuries
Pathophysiology and Pathoanatomy
Overview
Brachial plexus injuries (BPIs) are complex, life-altering injuries associated with considerable
physical, psychological, emotional, and economic effects.
The time from injury to management and the expected nerve regeneration time (depending
on the location of injury) ideally should be less than 18 months to prevent irreversible muscle
damage. For supraclavicular and proximal infraclavicular injuries involving innervation of the
intrinsic muscles of the hand, reliable reinnervation may be precluded.
A coordinated effort among surgeons, physiatrists, physical therapists, pain specialists, mental
health specialists, and social workers may help patients adjust to life after BPI.
BPI may result in various degrees of nerve injury and occasionally are associated with injuries
to more distal peripheral nerves.

Epidemiology
Most common in young men aged 15 and 30 years1,2
Usually associated with high-energy trauma (motor vehicle and motorcycle collisions)
70% involve injury to the nerve roots or trunks (supraclavicular)
Complete, pan-plexus injuries, which involve spinal nerves from all levels of the brachial
plexus (C5 through T1), are the most common type, with widely varying degrees of recovery
(approximately 75%).
Upper trunk injuries (C5-C6) account for approximately 23% of traumatic BPIs and typically
result from high-energy trauma that forces the shoulder in a caudal direction.
Lower trunk injuries (C7 through T1) account for approximately 2% of traumatic BPIs and
may result from forced shoulder abduction.1

Epidemiology
BPI often is associated with fractures and polytrauma.1 Patients typically are young,
working-age men engaged in high-risk behavior. Hong et al2 reported that 90.5% of
traumatic BPIs in the United States occurred in men, with a mean age of 26 years. The
incidence of BPI is increasing annually, likely because of an increase in extreme sports
and high-adventure activities and improved patient survival after severe high-energy and
multisystem trauma.1

Vascular Anatomy
Anastomotic networks between extraneural segmental arteries feeding the vasa nervorum
and the intraneural vascular network provide blood supply to nerves.
The cords of the brachial plexus derive their names from their spatial relationship to the
axillary artery.

Spinal nerve roots
The spinal nerve roots are formed from nerve rootlets that exit the spinal cord.
The dorsal root is the afferent sensory root. At the distal end of a dorsal root is a
coalescence of nerve cell bodies called the dorsal root ganglion (Figure 4), which conveys
sensory input to the spinal cord.
The ventral root (motor) joins the dorsal root distal to the dorsal root ganglion and forms
the spinal nerve. The cell bodies of the ventral root lie within the anterior horn of the spinal
cord gray matter.

types of injury: avulsion (B), stretch (C), and rupture (D). Traction to the brachial plexus may
cause nerve injuries of varying severity. Avulsion (preganglionic) injuries of the nerve roots
from the spinal cord cannot, for practical purposes, be repaired. With stretch
(postganglionic) injuries, some spontaneous recovery is possible. Extraforaminal rupture of
the nerve or trunk can be repaired surgically. (Reproduced with permission from the Mayo
Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Injury location
Lesions that occur proximal to the dorsal root ganglion are referred to as preganglionic or
supraganglionic.
Lesions distal to the dorsal root ganglion are referred to as postganglionic or
infraganglionic.
Anatomy pearls
Terminal nerve branches that arise from the root level are clinically important because they
may indicate the level of the lesion.

These include the phrenic nerve (arising from C3 through C5), the dorsal scapular nerve to
the rhomboid muscles arising from C5, and the long thoracic nerve to the serratus anterior
muscle (arising from C5 through C7).
If these muscles function and paralysis of the arm is present distally, injury to the brachial
plexus must have occurred distal to their take-off of the associated nerve root (ie,
postganglionic).
The only terminal nerve branch off the trunk level is the suprascapular nerve (innervating the
infraspinatus and supraspinatus), which branches off the upper trunk at the Erb point, at
which the upper trunk emerges between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
No terminal branches are present off the division level, aside from the suprascapular nerve,
which often trifurcates with the posterior and anterior divisions of the upper trunk.
Tendons
Muscles and tendons should be examined.
Concurrent tendon injuries may need to be addressed before management of BPI.
Joints and Ligaments
Joints and ligaments may be injured concurrently or they may become stiff over time.
Home exercises and hand therapy may help protect the joints during recovery.
Musculature
The brachial plexus supplies all motor and sensory function to the upper extremity (Table 1),
and the level of injury will correlate with specific deficits.
Weakness and heaviness of the arm may result from lack of motor nerve input.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The brachial plexus is formed from the intertwining of the peripheral nerves that
originate from the anterior rami of the C5 throughT1 spinal nerve roots and, to a lesser
extent, from C4 (prefixed) and T2 (postfixed). It passes from the spine laterally through
the posterior triangle of the neck, over the first rib, and into the axilla before branching

9/4/26, 10:13 AM
AAOS | Nerve Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000559
9/128

into peripheral nerves that supply the shoulder muscles and then to the arm to
innervate the muscles, skin, and soft tissues of the arm and hand.3
The brachial plexus is divided into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal branches.
Ventral and dorsal rootlets combine to form the spinal nerves. The C5 through C7 roots
are attached to their corresponding vertebral transverse processes by epineurial fibers,
which help stabilize these roots and make them less susceptible to avulsion injuries than
the more distal roots.4
Typically, the C5 and C6 nerve roots converge just lateral to the anterior scalene muscle
at the Erb point, approximately 2 cm cranial to the clavicle, forming the upper trunk,
whereas the C8 and T1 roots become the lower trunk between the middle and posterior
scalene muscles, and the C7 root continues as the middle trunk. Anterior and posterior
divisions of each trunk emerge before crossing deep to the clavicle. The anterior
divisions of the upper and middle trunks combine to form the lateral cord. The medial
cord arises from the anterior division of the lower trunk, and the posterior cord is
formed by the three posterior divisions. The cords derive their names from their location
in relation to the axillary artery distal to the coracoid process. They then continue into
the extremity, forming the terminal branches that make up the major nerves of the
upper extremity.4
A few nerves branch directly from various locations along the plexus. From the C5 nerve
root, the phrenic and dorsal scapular nerves arise, with the long thoracic nerve forming
from contributions of the C5 through C7 nerve roots. The nerve to the subclavius and
suprascapular nerve (Erb point) arises from the upper trunk. The lateral and medial
pectoral nerves are branches from the lateral and medial cords, respectively, and the
medial cord also gives off the medial brachial cutaneous and medial antebrachial
cutaneous nerves. Posterior cord branches include the thoracodorsal and subscapular
nerves.4
Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
BPI may occur secondary to traction, compression, and/or penetrating injuries.

The cause of a BPI may inform the severity of injury and the treatment plans. BPI usually
results from high-energy trauma. The worldwide increase in BPIs is thought to result from the
increased popularity of high-energy sports and increased survival after motor vehicle collisions
secondary to safety mechanisms, such as airbags.
Motor vehicle collisions are the leading cause of traumatic BPIs worldwide. The approximate
rule of seven seventies is an approximating mnemonic device that may help surgeons
remember the etiology and location of injuries.
70% of BPIs result from motor vehicle crashes, of which
70% involve bicycles or motorcycles.
70% of patients sustain multiple injuries.
70% of BPIs are supraclavicular.
At least 70% of patients with a supraclavicular injury have at least one nerve root avulsion.
70% of these injuries involve a lower root (C7, C8, T1).
In 70% of these patients, pain is an ongoing problem.
Direction of force on the upper extremity
Trauma that forces the arm/shoulder caudally (eg, a fall onto the shoulder; Figure 5) may
result in injuries that predominately affect the upper portions of the brachial plexus; however,
with enough energy, these injuries can disrupt all roots of the plexus.

Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
Traction on the brachial plexus may result from forces on the arm or shoulder girdle or
from forceful abduction of the arm. Energy directed in a caudal direction typically causes
injury of the superior roots, whereas forced abduction affects the inferior roots;
however, with enough force, all roots may be disrupted.5 More distally, nerves may be
injured via stretch, rupture, or laceration (directly from penetrating trauma or
secondarily from osseous fracture fragments). Sites at which branching occurs and
locations at which the brachial plexus is relatively fixed by surrounding tissues are more
prone to BPI.
Risk Factors
Male sex
Young age (15 to 30 years)
Trauma (motorcycle, motor vehicle, or all-terrain vehicle collisions; gunshot, knife, or other
penetrating injury; blast injury; crush injury)
Industrial workers
Risk-taking behavior/activities

Risk Factors
BPI may result from high-energy trauma, penetrating injury, blast injury, compression,
and/or iatrogenic causes along the course of the nerve fibers. Traction and transection
(including avulsion) are the two most common types of injuries that require surgical
management (some third-degree and sixth-degree; all fourth-degree and fifth-degree
injuries).
Associated Injuries
Polytrauma or multisystem injury

Cervical, first rib, clavicle, scapular fractures; fractures or dislocations of other nearby osseous
structures.
Vascular injury to adjacent vessels

Associated Injuries
Knowledge of associated injuries and adjacent anatomy aids in identifying the nerves at
risk. This information is especially important in patients with a fracture because fractures
may cause secondary injury to nerves as a result of laceration or compression from
increased swelling and compartment pressures. Similarly, nerves may be threatened by
joint dislocations. Chest wall trauma and injury to the spinal accessory nerve may affect
the potential extraplexal nerves that may serve as donors for nerve transfer. A thorough
patient history and physical examination and a review of imaging studies and treatment
options are key to understanding the mechanism of injury and associated injuries that
may affect the nerves and aid in preoperative planning.1,3
Injury Classification
Preganglionic versus postganglionic
Preganglionic BPIs, often referred to as root avulsions, are not repairable because the
rootlets are avulsed from the spinal cord. They are called preganglionic because the injury
has occurred proximal to the dorsal root ganglion.
Postganglionic BPIs occur distal to the dorsal root ganglion and can be repaired by restoring
nerve continuity, depending on the mechanism and location of injury. Mechanisms of injury
include laceration, penetrating injury, or traction (that results in rupture or stretch injury).
Level of injury—Multiple classification systems for BPIs have been devised. The most
descriptive system classifies BPIs according to the anatomic level of injury (Table 2).
Injuries often are multilevel, occurring between the two points in such a manner that the nerve
is fixed, restrained by surrounding structures, or changes in direction.
Supraclavicular injuries
C5 and C6 or upper trunk (Erb palsy) lesions account for approximately 20% to 25% of
traumatic BPIs.

The most common pattern of supraclavicular injury is complete involvement of all roots,

Injury Classification
BPIs are classified based on the anatomic location of the injury; however, many injuries
are multilevel and may fall into more than one category, depending on the classification
system used. BPIs may be described as preganglionic or postganglionic based on the
level involved or the nerve roots that are functionally affected. These distinctions are
important to make because they have implications with regard to patient prognosis and
available treatment options. Preganglionic nerve injuries occur between the dorsal root
ganglia and the spinal cord. These injuries are particularly devastating, and patient
prognosis is poor because injury is very proximal and few to no options exist for the
surgical repair of root avulsion injuries. Postganglionic injuries occur distal to the dorsal
root ganglia, and various treatment options are available, depending on the type and

and anatomic factors, which leads to highly variable outcomes. The level of nerve

Mechanism of injury

Patient History
The mechanism and timing of injury may help identify the type and level of injury, which
may direct treatment strategies. Some patients describe heaviness, possibly from a lack
of muscle strength and coordination of the shoulder girdle. A sling may help support
some of the load.
Physical Examination
Preganglionic lesions often cause more severe pain, dysesthesias, and paresthesia than
postganglionic lesions.
Possibly because of an associated spinal cord injury resulting from avulsion of the nerve
rootlets

are examined and documented systematically (Figure 7).

Every muscle of the upper extremity should be examined, with strength graded on a five-
point scale as described by the Medical Research Council (MRC) of the United Kingdom.
Although many variations and interpretations of the MRC grading system are available,
each surgeon can be consistent.
Key muscles to test are the rhomboids and the serratus anterior.
These muscles require special attention during the physical examination because injury to
their innervating nerves (the dorsal scapular nerve for the rhomboid muscles and the long
thoracic nerve for the serratus anterior muscle) indicates a supraclavicular and possibly a
preganglionic location of injury.
If these muscles are functional in patients with an upper plexus palsy, the lesion most likely
is postganglionic.

Physical Examination
After the acute, life- and limb-saving phase of care, a physical examination is performed
to localize the injury. This process is more difficult in patients with a complex, proximal
injury affecting multiple nerves and levels, such as a BPI.1,6 The patient is examined for
associated injuries, including soft-tissue and bony injuries of the affected extremities and
trauma to the head, neck, back, chest, and spine. Compartment syndrome should be
considered, given that diminished sensation may obscure the typical signs. If
compartment syndrome is possible, pressure measurements should be considered.
Specific tests and measurements, such as muscle and grip strength assessed via a
dynamometer, sensation testing via two-point discrimination, Semmes-Weinstein
monofilament testing, and tuning fork tests to assess vibratory sensation, may help
localize a lesion. Attempting to elicit a Tinel sign may indicate the level of injury and the
progress in recovery. In addition, careful documentation of physical examination
findings aids in overall team care because serial physical examinations are performed to
evaluate recovery and progress management.
Neurovascular Examination
Examination of the ipsilateral eye and eyelid

If T1 is avulsed (preganglionic injury), the sympathetic chain associated with the eye often is
injured, resulting in eyelid ptosis, meiosis (smaller pupil), and ipsilateral skin anhidrosis.
This condition is called Horner syndrome (Figure 8) and is pathognomonic for a
preganglionic T1 avulsion.

Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Radial, ulnar, brachial and axillary pulses
Evaluation of the radial, ulnar, brachial, and axillary pulses is important because arterial
injuries are quite common in patients with a complete BPI.
Arterial injuries also may result in a pseudoaneurysm, which may cause a pulsatile mass or
thrill on neurovascular examination.

Neurovascular Examination
All motor groups and sensory distributions innervated by the terminal branches of the
plexus are examined bilaterally and documented. Active and passive range of motion
(ROM) are documented. Motor strength and sensation are graded subjectively via the
MRC grading system.
Having the patient distinguish between sensation at the tip of the fingernail and on the
pulp of the finger (performed in a manner similar to that for two-point discrimination
testing) and performing the pick-up test, in which the patient is asked to reach for and
pick up an object, are simple and effective methods that can be used to evaluate

sensitivity and tactile gnosis.7 Abnormalities are confirmed and documented by
performing two-point discrimination, which is more objective.
Static and moving two-point discrimination measures the density of innervation. Normal
values are less than 6 mm for the palmar surface of the hand, and protective sensation
is defined as greater than 15 mm; however, results after nerve injury often are between
these two values.6 For other parts of the body, light touch can be used and graded
subjectively by the patient.
An advancing Tinel sign indicates nerve regeneration. Percussion over the nerve should
reproduce a tingling sensation in the anatomic distribution of the nerve. As nerve
recovery progresses distally, the Tinel sign also should advance, termed an advancing
Tinel sign. The maximum area at which tingling/paresthesia is elicited is thought to
represent the area of nerve injury (or nerve coaptation). The distalmost site at which
paresthesia can be elicited is thought to be the regenerative front of the nerve.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Chest radiographs and/or CT scans and CT scans of the cervical spine likely will be included in
the trauma workup and can aid in evaluation of injuries in proximity to the plexus.
Standard radiographs include views of the cervical spine, shoulder (AP and axillary views), and
chest to identify associated injuries.
Cervical spine radiographs are examined for cervical fracture.
Transverse process fractures of the cervical vertebrae may be associated with root avulsion
at the same level.
A chest radiograph may demonstrate a clavicle or rib fracture (first or second ribs), which
may be associated with damage to the adjacent brachial plexus.
Careful review of chest radiographs may reveal information on earlier rib fractures, which
may be important if intercostal nerves are considered for nerve transfers (rib fractures
often injure the associated intercostal nerves).
If the phrenic nerve is injured, associated paralysis of the hemidiaphragm will be observed.
A high probability of C5 root avulsion exists if diaphragmatic paralysis is noted.

Computed Tomography
CT myelography is the current preferred imaging modality for diagnosis of the level of nerve
root injury.
If a cervical root avulsion is present, the dural sheath heals with the development of a
pseudomeningocele.
Immediately postinjury, a blood clot often is found around the nerve root avulsion and may

Treatment Decisions
Timing of management
The time from injury to patient presentation determines whether nerve grafting or nerve
transfers can be performed.
Irreversible changes to the motor end plate occur without reestablishment of nerve
continuity, which is confounded by the slow regeneration of a nerve (1 mm/day) and the time
it takes to reach the motor end plate.
Nerve surgery is recommended within 6 months postinjury. After 12 months postinjury,
tendon transfers or FFMTs are considered.
Acute injuries
Sharp, penetrating injuries (eg, knife wounds) to the brachial plexus should be explored and
repaired acutely.
Vascular injuries associated with blunt trauma should be explored, and vessels should be
repaired or reconstructed. Nerve roots should be tagged for future identification and
reconstruction, if applicable.
Gunshot wounds should be observed because they typically are neurapraxic in nature.
Blunt trauma
Early management—If nerve root avulsions (preganglionic injuries) are suspected, surgical
management typically is recommended within 3 to 6 weeks postinjury.
Routine management—If a postganglionic injury (eg, rupture, stretch injury) is suspected,
delayed management (typically, 3 to 6 months postinjury) may allow for some recovery of
injured nerves (partial paralysis).
Late management
Patients who present between 6 and 12 months postinjury are in the late management
period.
Nerve transfers (neurotization) or nerve grafting are associated with poorer outcomes in
these patients than in patients who undergo early or routine management.

Indications
Surgical management is considered for root avulsions and neurotmetic injuries. High-

endoneural (Sunderland type 3 and type 4) and perineural sheaths (type 4). This causes

studies, and electrodiagnostic studies at appropriate intervals. Good clinical judgement
also is required to determine whether spontaneous recovery is plausible before
permanent denervation or whether the patient is likely to require surgical treatment to
achieve beneficial functional results. Therefore, surgical management also may be
considered if no clinical or electrophysiologic evidence of recovery is observed after 6
months of observation and sequential evaluation; however, such determinations are
more complex and associated with more potential for harm. The best opportunity for
return of function most often is an intact nerve and patience. Surgical management is
associated with the potential of disrupting recovering nerves about to show
improvement.
Contraindications
The major absolute contraindications to brachial plexus reconstruction are a patient’s
unwillingness to undergo surgical treatment and unrealistic patient goals.
Relative contraindications are severe elbow or shoulder contracture, advanced patient age,
medical comorbidities, and traumatic brain injury or cervical spinal cord injury.
Isolated C8-T1 BPIs also are a relative contraindication to brachial plexus reconstruction
because more predictable results may be achieved via distal nerve and/or tendon transfers.

Tendon transfers for radial nerve or posterior cord injuries are characterized as high or

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Successful tendon transfer depends on adhering to the two principles of tendon transfer
surgery to ensure that appropriate candidates are selected and that patients and tissues
are optimized for surgical treatment. The donor muscle is mobilized carefully, with care
taken to not disturb its neurovascular supply. The tendon should be aligned in a tunnel
of subcutaneous tissue that is healthy and free of fibrous attachments, which allows for
the smooth gliding of the tendon in alignment with the desired motor function. The
tendon should be weaved into its recipient tendon and assessed for alignment, tension,
and functionality by performing ROM testing about the joint. Postoperative
immobilization followed by a graduated physical therapy program is ideal for recovery
and re-education after tendon transfer surgery.

and more severe wound and medical complications.

Stability of the repair is critical in preventing tendon rupture or excessive stretching by placing
excessive tension on the repair site.
